guides.title: Ötzi and the Copper Age Alps
guides.description: Read the archaeological evidence from one traveller’s equipment, last meals, body and Alpine findspot.
guides.intro: A Copper Age man died near an Alpine pass almost 5,300 years before two hikers saw his body emerge from melting ice in 1991. He left an axe, a bow, clothing, food residues and other traces rarely preserved together. Each tells part of his history. The landscape, museum and laboratory archives also show how interpretations of his last journey and death have changed.
guides.scope: A close look at the man known as Ötzi, the site near Tisenjoch, and the evidence collected from his body and belongings. Modern discovery and research dates appear alongside independently dated Copper Age evidence.

map.scope: The Alpine divide, surrounding valleys and Bozen/Bolzano. Valley markers identify places discussed in research about the final ascent. Each is a broad landscape anchor.

sections.heading: A discovery at the Alpine watershed

paragraphs.text: Erika and Helmut Simon found the exposed body on 19 September 1991 while hiking in the Ötztal Alps. The find was initially treated as a comparatively recent death and Austrian responders helped recover it. A survey put the shallow hollow on the Italian side of a boundary close to the watershed. Further fieldwork recovered material from the ice and the hollow during successive visits. A bearskin cap recovered in the 1992 excavation is one reason to distinguish the first discovery from recovery of the assemblage.

sections.heading: How old was he?

paragraphs.text: Radiocarbon measurements on the remains place the man within 3350–3120 calibrated BCE. The range expresses the relationship between measured carbon and the calibration curve. It spans more than two centuries because a carbon measurement does not usually resolve an exact historical year. He lived in the Alpine Copper Age, when people worked copper and also depended heavily on stone, wood, hide and plant fibres. Estimates of about 45 years of age come from anatomical evidence and are a separate question from radiocarbon age.

sections.heading: The high hollow and changing ice

paragraphs.text: The body lay in a small depression near Tisenjoch at around 3,210 metres. Earlier descriptions emphasised protection from moving glacier ice. A later study re-examined the recovery records and nearby ice-core research and proposed that the location was repeatedly exposed or flooded during warm conditions. That model can account for some movement or altered positions of the artefacts after death. How often thaw exposed material and the precise initial positions of the body and objects remain open questions.

sections.heading: From plants to a proposed final ascent

paragraphs.text: A study recorded 75 kinds of moss and liverwort among materials from the find, many of which do not grow at the high-altitude hollow today. Researchers compared species from the soil, clothing and intestines with habitats elsewhere in the Alps. Together with pollen examined in different gut samples, the plants support a possible route northward through Val Senales, with changes of elevation in the earlier stages. Environmental distributions shifted after the Copper Age and people can carry plants indirectly. The evidence supports a corridor and an elevation sequence with room for more than one itinerary.

sections.heading: Food in the stomach

paragraphs.text: The stomach’s location was clarified in later imaging, making a new set of samples available separately from intestinal residues. Analysis of fats, proteins, DNA and microscopic remains linked the last meal to Alpine ibex, red deer and einkorn wheat. Researchers also found traces of bracken, whose role is unresolved. The meal contained a large proportion of fat, an energy-rich food in a high-altitude setting. A preserved meal is a short record of a person’s food rather than a full account of diet throughout life.

sections.heading: How the clothes were made

paragraphs.text: His surviving clothes include leggings, a coat, footwear, a cap and materials stitched from different hides. Mitochondrial DNA from sampled hides identified sheep and goat among components of the clothing, brown bear in the cap and roe deer in the quiver. A leather component of the footwear yielded cattle DNA. These objects show how domestic animals and hunted animals could contribute different materials to one traveller’s kit. Analyses identify particular samples and the clothing may have been repaired or remade over time.

sections.heading: An axe with a long material history

paragraphs.text: A haft of yew held a copper blade. Residue and construction details show that Late Neolithic or Copper Age builders combined materials with different mechanical properties. Lead isotope ratios in the copper matched ore sources in southern Tuscany better than others tested in the study. The result establishes a material connection between places far apart. Whether an axe, a blade, copper stock or material transferred through several hands travelled that distance remains unresolved.

sections.heading: Flint, a bow and work still in progress

paragraphs.text: Ötzi had a small stone-tool kit that included a dagger and arrowheads. Wear and chipped edges let researchers ask how pieces were made, used and sharpened. The bow that survived was unfinished, and the quiver contained both finished arrows and incomplete shafts. Flint studies link raw materials to more than one Alpine source area. Some pieces were heavily used or recently resharpened, yet the kit does not tell us how he had acquired each piece or why some equipment was unfinished.

sections.heading: An injury visible under the skin

paragraphs.text: Imaging revealed a stone arrowhead in the left shoulder region. An earlier CT study traced damage to the subclavian artery and proposed fatal haemorrhage. A 2025 reconstruction identified a local haematoma and considered whether the wound caused immediate death. Serious bleeding remains plausible, including bleeding outside the body, and the study leaves the time between injury and death open. A wound on his hand and debated signs of head injury add context. They do not identify another person, a motive or a complete order of events.

sections.heading: Tattoos, joints and a stomach microbe

paragraphs.text: Multispectral imaging helped researchers map 61 tattoos, mainly lines and crosses. Some lie near joints affected by degenerative changes. A possible therapeutic purpose has been proposed, while the social meaning and technique of each mark cannot be read straight from its location. An ancient genome of Helicobacter pylori was also recovered from his stomach. It gives researchers evidence about the bacterium’s history and his exposure to it, with different evidence needed to establish which symptoms he experienced.

sections.heading: What the new genome changed

paragraphs.text: The high-coverage genome published in 2023 reduced problems from contamination that affected earlier genetic work. Statistical models found an unusually high proportion of ancestry related to early Anatolian farmers among the European comparisons used, and no detectable steppe-related ancestry in that model. Variants also suggested relatively dark skin and a predisposition to male-pattern baldness. Phenotype probabilities and ancestry estimates refer to one individual and depend on the samples and models used. They cannot assign a modern national or ethnic identity to the man.

sections.heading: Keeping a person and his things in care

paragraphs.text: The South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology maintains a cold chamber and monitors the body’s environment. Conservation takes continuing observation, because even well-preserved tissue and organic materials are vulnerable once recovered. Photography and three-dimensional records allow certain spatial questions to be examined without repeatedly moving the remains. The map separates the recovery area from the museum so an institutional address never stands in for an ancient location.

sections.heading: Claims and the evidence behind them

cells: When did he live?
Radiocarbon dates on remains, calibrated to 3350–3120 BCE.
A date range for the man’s lifetime and death.
Where was his body found?
Documented site near Tisenjoch at about 3,210 metres.
A recovery location. The exact place where he died remains uncertain.
What had he eaten?
Stomach microscopy and molecular evidence, including ibex, deer and einkorn.
A window onto one meal. Bracken’s role is unresolved.
How did his copper arrive?
Lead isotope comparisons link axe copper to southern Tuscany.
The likely ore region. The archaeological pathway remains open.
Was the arrow wound fatal?
Imaging located the arrowhead, arterial damage and a haematoma.
A severe injury with uncertain timing, blood loss and interaction with other injuries.
Did the ice stay unchanged?
Neighbouring ice records and recovery documentation support multiple taphonomic models.
The preservation history could include episodes of exposure, melt and movement.

guides.title: People preserved in cold landscapes
guides.description: Compare glacier recoveries, dry Arctic graves and ice-filled Altai burial chambers across the Northern Hemisphere.
guides.intro: Cold can preserve clothing, hair, food residues and skin, but the circumstances differ from place to place. Some people died while travelling and were recovered from ice or meltwater. Others were buried by their communities and preserved in dry graves or frozen chambers. The histories of who studied, cared for and returned these people differ as much as their preservation.
guides.scope: Selected northern cases from the Alps, Greenland, northwestern North America and the Altai. The companion Andean guide treats high-elevation Inca offerings separately.

map.scope: Wide northern comparison across modern continents. Pins distinguish regional recovery localities, settlement anchors and modern collections. The Tatshenshini-Alsek point represents the park region.

sections.heading: Three preservation settings

paragraphs.text: In a glacier or ice patch, cold can slow decay and help preserve material exposed again by melting. In a sheltered grave, cold and dry air can contribute to dehydration. At Pazyryk, ice developed inside burial chambers and preserved deposits assembled through burial rites. These processes sometimes act together, and surviving material can deteriorate quickly after exposure. Archaeologists ask how a body reached its setting, where cold acted, and which materials later moved.

sections.heading: Ötzi and the Tisenjoch hollow

paragraphs.text: Ötzi died in the late fourth millennium BCE. Hikers found him in 1991 near the Austria–Italy border. A shallow hollow and changing snow and ice protected many of his belongings. Research continues into whether the find underwent repeated episodes of melt, exposure and displacement. It is possible to read the arrow wound and compare the materials in his toolkit even when the precise way the body reached the hollow is unresolved.

sections.heading: A traveller of another Alpine age

paragraphs.text: Coins, shoes, arms and equipment from the Theodul glacier in Switzerland point to an early modern traveller, with the coins supporting a date around 1600. This was a different period of travel and trade across the Alps, and the assemblage speaks through objects with a different material history. The familiar label “mercenary” is a historical nickname. The traveller’s occupation remains uncertain and the objects’ movements in the ice make their original arrangement difficult to reconstruct.

sections.heading: A community burial near Uummannaq

paragraphs.text: At Qilakitsoq, two graves held six women and two boys buried in skins and clothing. Greenland’s National Museum and Archives dates the burial group to around 1475 and discusses family relationships spanning the two graves. Hans and Jokum Grønvold found them in 1972. Dry and cold conditions in the sheltered graves preserved several of the people. The death of all eight has no established single explanation. The burial grouping describes how they were cared for after death.

sections.heading: Garments, skin and change after recovery

paragraphs.text: Inuit seamstresses selected and worked animal skins into garments suited to Arctic conditions. The graves preserved details of seams, layering and how garments fit together. The evidence also includes amulets and skin markings. Conservation investigations after recovery addressed damage from fungi, an illustration of how organisms and humidity can become problems under new conditions. Each current display and research collection has a different history from the people’s original clothing and burial.

sections.heading: A person found in Champagne and Aishihik territory

paragraphs.text: In 1999, hunters encountered frozen remains in the Tatshenshini-Alsek region. Champagne and Aishihik First Nations led work concerning the person they named Kwäday Dän Ts’ìnchi, often translated as Long Ago Person Found. Radiocarbon modelling that combined bone collagen with a robe put the man between about 1670 and 1850 calibrated CE. Earlier dates on associated objects had suggested a different age. Marine foods affect radiocarbon interpretation, and objects that appear together after melting can have entered the landscape at different times.

sections.heading: What food sources say about travel

paragraphs.text: Bone chemistry indicates substantial marine food in his longer-term diet, even though the glacier was well inland. Evidence from plants and animals recovered in the investigation helps connect parts of his recent experience with coast and mountain environments. Marine isotope signatures can reflect food transferred through trade or carried on a journey. They are one component of a reconstruction that includes material evidence and Indigenous knowledge of travel through the region.

sections.heading: Family connections and responsibility

paragraphs.text: The Champagne and Aishihik First Nations community DNA study reported 17 relatives from Yukon and Alaska. The project’s public records discuss the family finding, community events and knowledge about the land. The biological evidence can support recognition of a maternal relationship. Contemporary kinship, care, knowledge and authority also come from the community, which set priorities for work on the find and directed commemoration and return.

sections.heading: Burial ice at Pazyryk

paragraphs.text: Altai burial mounds contained wooden chambers and carefully assembled grave deposits. In several mounds water froze within or around the chambers and ice protected felt, leather, wood, textiles and the remains of people and horses. Some human bodies had also undergone deliberate funeral preparation. Post-burial freezing and cultural preparation each contributed to what survived, alongside disturbance and excavation. The distribution is uneven even within one cemetery.

sections.heading: Ukok and the debates about care

paragraphs.text: The individual from Ak-Alakha-3 on the Ukok Plateau is connected to the broader Pazyryk archaeological tradition, in a different burial and landscape from the Pazyryk cemetery. Following research in Novosibirsk, her body returned to the Anokhin National Museum in Gorno-Altaisk in 2012. Ethnographic research describes disputes about display, return and ways of caring for her. Many Indigenous Altai people opposed public display. A regional guide can teach about the burial through its landscape, documented material context and the positions expressed by people with relationships to it.

sections.heading: What an image can reveal or expose

paragraphs.text: Near-infrared recording of a tattooed woman from Pazyryk Barrow 5 clarified darkened designs and showed differences in the way parts of the tattoos were made. The work addresses marks on a particular individual, with technique inferred from detail rather than observing the act itself. Research images provide evidence in a scientific setting, while whether and how to show people’s remains publicly remains a question of care and community authority. The map uses landscapes and place descriptions to support comparison.

sections.heading: How the cases differ

cells: Ötzi
A high Alpine hollow influenced by ice, snow and meltwater.
Direct calibrated radiocarbon range. Subsequent movement and exposure are under study.
Theodul traveller
Glacier finds from an Alpine crossing, including fragments of human remains and possessions.
Coins date the assemblage to around 1600. The traveller’s occupation remains uncertain.
Qilakitsormiut
Deliberate Inuit burials, with cold and drying in a sheltered setting.
Burial context, radiocarbon and textile studies. Cause of death unresolved.
Kwäday Dän Ts’ìnchi
Glacier recovery in community territory, with clothing and other objects.
Combined robe and bone dates, with attention to marine diet and possible multiple episodes of site use.
Pazyryk and Ukok
Natural ice in chambers prepared for burial, at distinct localities.
Archaeology, wood and associated artefacts. Dating and mortuary practice vary by mound.
